(CNN) -- Human rights groups in Bangladesh and abroad are calling for an investigation after 16 borders guards accused of participating in a bloody revolt in February died in custody in recent days. A Bangladesh Rifles soldier is shown wearing a white cloth signifying surrender in late February. The Bangladesh military acknowledged the deaths of the Bangladesh Rifles paramilitary troops, or jawans -- but insisted they were the result of illness and suicide. "Given the history of abuses by security forces in Bangladesh, there is no reason to take at face value the claim that these detainees have committed suicide," said Brad Adams, Asia director or the New York-based Human Rights Watch, in a statement. The 16 were among 1,100 jawans rounded up after a 35-hour mutiny that began on February 25 in the Rifles headquarters in the capital city, Dhaka. The jawans rebelled against their commanding officers, taking dozens of them hostage. When the standoff ended, more than 70 people were found dead -- the majority of them army officers. Initially, Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina promised the jawans amnesty if they laid down their arms. But once the scope of the massacre came to light, Hasina withdrew her offer -- saying the government will not show mercy to those who killed, looted or committed arson. The jawans were issued an ultimatum to turn themselves in, while the government created a committee to probe into the mutiny. The result of the government inquiry is yet to be made public, after several delays. On Thursday, the Rifles leadership issued a statement that said 16 detainees have died in custody since March 9: four from suicide, six from heart attacks and six from other diseases. "We believe that perhaps they have failed to cope with the mental pressure associated with the guilt of committing the brutal attacks,"the statement said. It then added: "Suicide is seen as a sin in religious terms and is also socially undesirable." In response, the legal aid group, Ain o Salish Kendro (Law and Adjudication Center), and the Bangladesh National Women Lawyers' Association were among several organizations calling for an investigation. During a hearing Wednesday, one of the suspects told a Dhaka court he had been administered electric shocks during a seven-day detention. Family members of other detainees have made similar allegations. Some of the suspects who died in custody had wounds on their bodies consisted with torture, Human Rights Watch said. Bangladeshi authorities have said the wounds may have been inflicted when the suspects tried to escape from the Rifles headquarters after the rebellion. "The explanations given by representatives of the security forces are simply not credible," Adams said. "Torture is a regular 'investigative technique' in Bangladesh and killing of detains in government custody is an endemic problem." The country's elite anti-crime unit, Rapid Action Battalion (RAB), have often been accused of 'extra-judicial' killings. The battalion is involved in the interrogation of many of the Rifles suspects. Since its inception in 2004, more than 550 alleged criminals died soon after they were captured by RAB forces. In each case, the battalion claimed the arrested men died from stray bullets as their units were engaged in gun battles with the suspects' comrades. The 65,000-strong Bangladesh Rifles is responsible primarily for guarding the country's borders, but it also takes part in operations such as monitoring polls. It is distinct from the army, but their commanders are career army officers. The troops staged their rebellion on the second day of BDR Week, when officers and troops from various BDR outposts along the border were in the capital for celebrations. Discontent had been bubbling for years in the ranks of the BDR, who complained their army superiors dismissed their appeals for more pay, subsidized food and their requests to participate in United Nations peacekeeping operations -- which pay far more than what they make at home. Bangladesh and its South Asian neighbors are the largest troop contributors to U.N. peacekeeping operations. During the stand-off, dozens of officers were killed. Some bodies were dumped in mass graves. Others were tossed in sewers that emptied into a river, where they floated for miles before being retrieved.

**Human rights groups call for probe into deaths of Bangladesh mutiny suspects in custody**

*Dhaka, Bangladesh* — Human rights groups are calling on Bangladeshi authorities to investigate the deaths in custody of soldiers accused of taking part in the bloody February 2009 mutiny by members of the Bangladesh Rifles, saying allegations of torture and abuse must be fully examined.

The mutiny, which began at the paramilitary force’s headquarters in Dhaka and spread to other units, left dozens dead, including many army officers. Thousands of Bangladesh Rifles personnel were later detained and prosecuted in connection with the uprising, one of the most serious security crises in the country’s recent history.

Rights advocates say a number of detained soldiers have died while in custody since the crackdown began. They have urged the government to ensure independent autopsies, make findings public and hold any officials responsible for abuse accountable.

“The authorities have an obligation to explain how detainees died while under state control,” one rights campaigner said. “If torture or mistreatment occurred, those responsible must be prosecuted.”

Bangladesh’s government has previously said it is committed to bringing those behind the mutiny to justice and has maintained that legal proceedings are being conducted through proper channels. Officials have also described the uprising as a grave attack on state institutions and the chain of command.

But human rights organizations have raised concerns about the scale of the arrests, conditions of detention and the fairness of some proceedings. They say the seriousness of the mutiny does not diminish the government’s duty to protect detainees’ rights.

The Bangladesh Rifles, a border security force, was later reorganized and renamed Border Guard Bangladesh.

Families of some detainees have alleged that their relatives were tortured during interrogation or denied adequate medical treatment. Rights groups say such claims underscore the need for a transparent investigation separate from the security agencies involved in the arrests.

The 2009 mutiny shocked Bangladesh and left deep scars within the military and security establishment. The trials that followed became among the largest in the country’s history, with mass convictions and lengthy prison sentences handed down to many former members of the force.

Human rights groups say accountability must extend not only to the killings committed during the mutiny, but also to any abuses committed during the government’s response.

“The victims of the mutiny deserve justice,” the campaigner said. “But justice cannot be achieved through unlawful detention, torture or deaths in custody.”

counterfactuals.output:
## After the Bangladesh Rifles Revolt: Detainee Deaths, Torture Allegations, and the Government’s Response

**Dhaka, Bangladesh** — The aftermath of the 2009 Bangladesh Rifles revolt in Dhaka has remained one of the most contentious chapters in Bangladesh’s recent history, marked not only by the scale of the mutiny and killings inside the paramilitary force’s headquarters but also by allegations of custodial deaths, torture, and due-process violations during the government’s sweeping crackdown.

The revolt, which began on **25 February 2009** at the Bangladesh Rifles headquarters in **Pilkhana, Dhaka**, left **74 people dead**, including **57 army officers** seconded to command the border force. The violence shocked the country and triggered a massive security operation, followed by the detention of thousands of BDR personnel and civilians suspected of involvement.

In the years that followed, the government pursued one of the largest criminal justice processes in Bangladesh’s history. But human rights groups, lawyers, and families of detainees have repeatedly alleged that the state’s response was marred by torture, forced confessions, and deaths in custody.

### Mass Arrests After the Mutiny

Following the revolt, authorities detained large numbers of BDR members from Pilkhana and other units across the country. Many were interrogated by police, the Rapid Action Battalion, intelligence agencies, and other security bodies.

The government divided the legal response into multiple tracks. Thousands of BDR personnel were tried under internal mutiny proceedings for disciplinary offences, while hundreds faced criminal charges including murder, conspiracy, looting, arson, and desecration of bodies.

The criminal case over the Pilkhana killings eventually became one of the largest murder trials in the world by number of accused. In **2013**, a Dhaka court sentenced **152 people to death**, hundreds more to life imprisonment or other prison terms, and acquitted others. Subsequent appeals modified some verdicts, but the cases remained controversial because of the size and complexity of the proceedings.

### Detainee Deaths Raise Alarm

One of the most serious concerns involved deaths of BDR detainees while in custody or shortly after interrogation.

Human rights organizations reported that dozens of suspected mutineers died after being detained. Rights groups including **Human Rights Watch**, **Amnesty International**, and Bangladeshi organizations such as **Odhikar** documented allegations that many deaths followed severe mistreatment, torture, or denial of medical care.

Some official accounts described the deaths as resulting from illness, heart attacks, suicide, or other natural causes. Families of detainees and rights activists disputed many of those explanations, saying bodies bore signs of injury and that detainees had been tortured during interrogation.

Reports from the period described alleged methods including beatings, electric shocks, suspension, sleep deprivation, and other forms of physical and psychological abuse. Lawyers and relatives said some detainees were held incommunicado, denied timely access to counsel, or pressured into confessing.

The government acknowledged some detainee deaths but generally rejected claims of systematic torture. Officials said deaths were investigated and that the state was committed to prosecuting those responsible for the mutiny and killings.

### Torture Allegations and Forced Confessions

A recurring allegation was that confessions used in prosecutions were obtained under coercion. Defence lawyers argued that many accused BDR members were tortured until they admitted involvement or implicated others. Some defendants later retracted confessions in court, claiming they had been forced.

Human rights groups raised concerns that the scale of the prosecutions made individualized justice difficult. They argued that the authorities needed to distinguish between those directly involved in killings, those who participated in the mutiny, and those who were merely present at the compound or in BDR service at the time.

The government maintained that the cases were handled through the courts and that defendants had access to legal remedies. Prosecutors argued that the brutality of the Pilkhana killings required a firm legal response and that evidence included witness testimony, forensic findings, and recovered weapons.

### Families Caught Between Grief and Accusation

The tragedy created two sets of grieving families.

The families of the murdered army officers demanded justice for what they described as a planned massacre. Many of them said the mutiny was not merely a pay-and-grievance uprising but a coordinated attack targeting army officers. Their demands placed heavy pressure on the newly elected government of Prime Minister **Sheikh Hasina**, which had taken office only weeks before the revolt.

At the same time, families of detained BDR personnel said their relatives were collectively blamed, tortured, and in some cases killed before receiving a fair trial. Some said they struggled for years to obtain information about detained relatives or to challenge confessions allegedly extracted through abuse.

### Government Response and Rebranding of the Force

The Bangladesh government responded to the revolt by restructuring the paramilitary force. The Bangladesh Rifles was renamed the **Border Guard Bangladesh** under a new law aimed at reforming command structures, discipline, and operations.

Officials said the reforms were intended to prevent future breakdowns in discipline and restore public confidence in the border force. The government also emphasized that the trials demonstrated its commitment to accountability for the killings at Pilkhana.

However, rights groups criticized the government for failing to adequately investigate allegations of custodial abuse. They called for independent inquiries into every detainee death, prosecution of security personnel involved in torture, and exclusion of coerced confessions from trial proceedings.

### International and Domestic Criticism

International human rights bodies repeatedly urged Bangladesh to ensure that prosecutions met fair-trial standards. They warned that the death penalty verdicts, the large number of accused tried together, and allegations of torture could undermine the legitimacy of the process.

Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch called on the authorities to investigate custodial deaths and torture claims impartially. Domestic rights groups similarly argued that justice for the murdered officers should not come at the expense of basic rights for the accused.

Bangladesh’s authorities responded that the courts were independent and that the accused had opportunities to appeal. They also pointed to the scale of the atrocity committed during the mutiny and the need to maintain discipline within the armed and paramilitary forces.

### A Legacy Still Contested

More than a decade later, the Pilkhana revolt remains deeply sensitive in Bangladesh. For the military establishment and the families of slain officers, it was an act of betrayal and brutality requiring severe punishment. For human rights advocates, the state’s response exposed enduring problems of custodial abuse, weak accountability for security forces, and reliance on confessions in criminal investigations.

The government’s official position has emphasized justice for the victims of the mutiny and institutional reform of the border force. But unresolved questions over detainee deaths and torture allegations continue to shadow the legacy of the case.

The revolt itself lasted only about two days. Its aftermath — in courtrooms, prisons, military institutions, and grieving households — has lasted far longer.

**Bangladesh Rifles mutiny still casts shadow over Sheikh Hasina era as custody-death allegations haunt crackdown**

DHAKA, Bangladesh — More than a decade after a bloody mutiny by members of the Bangladesh Rifles stunned the country and shook the newly elected government of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, the uprising remains one of Bangladesh’s most traumatic security crises — not only for the scale of the killings inside the border force’s Dhaka headquarters, but also for what followed: mass arrests, sweeping trials and persistent allegations that detainees were tortured or died in custody.

The mutiny began on Feb. 25, 2009, at the Bangladesh Rifles headquarters in Pilkhana, a densely populated area of the capital. Members of the paramilitary border force, then known as the BDR, rose up against their army officers during an annual gathering, taking hostages and opening fire. By the time the rebellion was brought under control the next day, 74 people had been killed, including 57 army officers, making it one of the deadliest episodes in Bangladesh’s military history.

The revolt posed an immediate test for Hasina, who had returned to power only weeks earlier after elections ended two years of army-backed caretaker rule. Her government negotiated with the mutineers before security forces reasserted control. Authorities later said the rebellion had been driven by grievances over pay, benefits and command structures, though the brutality of the killings — including the discovery of bodies in mass graves and sewers — shocked the public and devastated the military establishment.

In the aftermath, the government launched one of the largest criminal investigations and prosecution efforts in the country’s history. Thousands of BDR personnel were detained. The force was later reorganized and renamed Border Guard Bangladesh. Hundreds of members were tried in special courts for mutiny-related offenses, while a separate mass murder case led to death sentences for scores of defendants and prison terms for many others.

But the crackdown soon drew scrutiny from human rights organizations, lawyers and families of the accused. Rights groups alleged that security agencies, including the Rapid Action Battalion, known as RAB, and police intelligence units, abused detainees during interrogations. Former detainees and relatives described beatings, electric shocks, forced confessions and prolonged detention without adequate legal access. The government has denied systematic abuse and said prosecutions followed the law.

Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and Bangladeshi rights organizations repeatedly called for investigations into the reported deaths of BDR suspects in custody. Human Rights Watch said dozens of detainees died after arrest, citing accounts that some had shown signs of torture or ill-treatment. Local groups also documented cases in which families alleged that men taken into custody by law enforcement or paramilitary units were later returned dead or seriously injured.

Officials at the time often attributed the deaths to natural causes, including heart attacks or illness. Rights advocates argued that the number of deaths, their timing and the lack of transparent independent inquiries raised serious concerns. They said the authorities had an obligation to investigate not only the mutiny killings but also any abuse committed during the state’s response.

The trials themselves were also criticized. While many Bangladeshis demanded justice for the slain officers and their families, human rights lawyers said the mass nature of the proceedings risked undermining due process. Hundreds of defendants were tried together, and rights groups questioned whether all suspects had meaningful access to counsel or the opportunity to challenge evidence allegedly obtained under coercion.

The legacy of the mutiny has remained politically sensitive. For Hasina’s government, the handling of the crisis was presented as an effort to stabilize the country, prevent wider bloodshed and punish those responsible for the massacre. For the families of the slain officers, the prosecutions were a necessary response to an atrocity that decapitated much of the BDR’s army command structure. For families of accused border guards, however, the years after Pilkhana brought grief of a different kind: arrests, lengthy imprisonment, death sentences and unanswered questions about men who died before they could fully defend themselves.

The Rapid Action Battalion, an elite anti-crime and counterterrorism force, has long been accused by rights organizations of extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances and torture in separate cases across Bangladesh. Those broader allegations intensified international scrutiny of the BDR mutiny aftermath, especially as detainee-abuse claims emerged. RAB has denied unlawful conduct, and successive Bangladeshi governments have defended the force as essential to national security.

The mutiny’s consequences still reverberate through Bangladesh’s military, legal and political institutions. It left the country mourning dozens of officers, transformed the border force and produced years of litigation. Yet the custody-death allegations remain an unresolved chapter. Human rights organizations continue to argue that justice for the victims of the Pilkhana massacre should not come at the expense of accountability for torture or deaths in detention.

For Bangladesh, the events of February 2009 are remembered as both a national security catastrophe and a test of the rule of law — one in which the demand for punishment collided with enduring questions about how the state treated those it accused.

(CNN) -- Human rights groups in Bangladesh have demanded an independent investigation into the deaths of several detained border guards accused of taking part in February’s bloody uprising, saying the circumstances have raised serious concerns about possible abuse in custody.

The groups said the deaths of the Bangladesh Rifles jawans — the rank-and-file border guards — must be investigated transparently and that post-mortem findings should be made public.

The February mutiny at the Bangladesh Rifles headquarters in Dhaka shocked the country and left dozens of people dead, including many army officers. Authorities later arrested large numbers of border guards suspected of involvement in the uprising.

Rights activists said that while those responsible for killings during the revolt should face justice, detainees must be protected under the law.

“No crime can justify torture or custodial death,” rights campaigners said, urging the government to ensure due process and accountability.

Officials have said investigations into the uprising are continuing. Authorities have previously described some of the deaths among detained jawans as suicides or the result of illness, but rights groups and families of the accused have questioned those explanations.

The mutiny began in late February when Bangladesh Rifles personnel turned on their commanding officers at the force’s headquarters. The uprising spread to other border posts before ending after government negotiations and mass surrenders.

The government has promised trials for those accused of murder, looting and rebellion. Human rights organizations, however, have warned that the scale of the arrests and the highly charged atmosphere surrounding the case make independent oversight essential.
